local_facts.claim: Florida Rule of Criminal Procedure 3.130 requires that every arrested person not already released in a lawful manner be taken before a judicial officer within 24 hours of arrest, in person or by electronic audiovisual device at the court's discretion. At that hearing the judge must state the charge, provide a copy of the complaint, and advise the person of the right to remain silent and the right to counsel. Rule 3.133 sets a separate 48-hour limit for a nonadversary probable cause determination when the defendant is in custody.
local_facts.why_it_matters: In Hillsborough County that hearing is normally run by video link from the county jail, and release conditions are addressed at it. Rule 3.130(c)(2) also requires the judge to allow a defendant who is hiring counsel reasonable time to send for that lawyer and, on request, to have an officer carry a message to a named lawyer inside the county at no cost. That makes the first day after an arrest the point at which counsel matters most.
local_facts.title: A judge is supposed to see an arrested person within 24 hours

local_facts.claim: Administrative Order S-2025-063 of the Thirteenth Judicial Circuit adopts the statewide uniform bond schedule for Hillsborough County without change, effective January 1 through December 31, 2026. The order states the schedule applies only to the booking officer and does not bind a judge, and it excludes a long list of arrests, including capital, life, first- and second-degree felonies, homicide, felony battery, domestic battery by strangulation, domestic violence under Florida Statutes 741.28, stalking, robbery, burglary, carjacking, kidnapping, trafficking in a controlled substance, violation of a protective injunction, anyone on pretrial release, probation or community control at the time of a felony arrest, and anyone arrested three or more times in the preceding six months.
local_facts.why_it_matters: It decides whether anyone can be bonded out at the jail counter or has to wait for a judge. For every excluded charge there is no pre-first-appearance release, and the judge then makes an individualized determination under Florida Statutes 903.011(6) and 903.046 and Rule 3.131. Prior supervision status and recent arrest history change the answer even when the charge itself is minor.
local_facts.title: The 2026 Hillsborough bond schedule binds the booking officer, not the judge

local_facts.claim: The Hillsborough County Clerk of Court states that after a felony arrest the county jail sends the initial paperwork to the Clerk's felony department, which prepares the official court file including the original arrest document and any release forms and forwards it to the Office of the State Attorney, which then determines whether to file formal charges. Once charges are filed with the Clerk, the defendant is notified by mail of an arraignment date, sent to the address provided at the time of arrest, and the bail bond agent is also notified if the defendant bonded out. The felony department cannot change a court date once notice has gone out.
local_facts.why_it_matters: An arrest is not a filed charge, and the gap between them is where people assume a case has gone away. The notice that resumes it goes to whatever address was recorded at booking, so anyone who moved, or who gave a temporary address, can miss a court date they never saw. Missing it does not pause the case.
local_facts.title: The arraignment date is mailed to the address you gave at arrest

anchors.label: Application fee for court-appointed counsel
anchors.detail: Anyone asking the Hillsborough Clerk to declare them indigent so a public defender can be appointed owes this fee on each application, due within seven days of filing it.

anchors.label: Statutory court costs on a felony conviction
anchors.detail: Assessed as a cost in the case on a plea or a finding of guilt, on top of any fine. The same schedule sets $60 for a misdemeanor and $60 for a criminal traffic offense.

anchors.label: Income line for public defender eligibility
anchors.detail: The Clerk must find an applicant indigent when household income sits at or below 200 percent of the current federal poverty guideline for that household size.

anchors.label: Court costs, county or municipal ordinance prosecution
anchors.detail: The Hillsborough Clerk's published fee list puts the misdemeanor-side court cost imposed on a non-prevailing party in a county or municipal prosecution at this figure.
anchors.source_name: Hillsborough Clerk of Court fee list

fee_rows.stage: A defense fee tied to the outcome
fee_rows.note: Rule 4-1.5(f)(3)(B) forbids a lawyer from arranging for, charging, or collecting a contingency fee for representing a defendant in a criminal matter.

fee_rows.share: $15,000 life · $10,000 first or second degree · $5,000 third degree
fee_rows.note: Ceilings a judge cannot exceed unless another statute authorizes more or the amount doubles pecuniary gain or loss. A fine is separate from costs.
Same statute, lower tiers. Second-degree ceiling also covers a noncriminal violation, and a withheld adjudication still counts as a conviction for it.
Paid to the Clerk per application. Unpaid, it is assessed at sentencing or as a probation condition, and the first $50 of any money paid is applied to it.

fee_rows.stage: Attorney fee lien after a conviction with appointed counsel
fee_rows.note: A conviction after public defender representation carries a statutory fee judgment, imposed regardless of present ability to pay, and a court may set more on proof.
